summary: Chinese joins clauses with linking words that often come in pairs — and the word order inside a clause never changes. ‘But’ is 但是 or, more spoken, 可是, at the start of the second clause. ‘Because … so’ is 因为…，所以… — reason first, often both halves marked. ‘Although’ is 虽然…，但是 / 可是… — again both halves. ‘If’ is 如果…（的话），…就… with 就 after the subject of the result, right before its verb; ‘then’ is 然后. ‘When’ is …的时候, which comes AFTER its clause: 我饿的时候 ‘when I’m hungry’. There is no ‘that’: 我知道他是老师 ‘I know (that) he is a teacher’. And 和 ‘and’ joins nouns, never clauses. Unlike German, no verb moves to the end: 因为我很累 keeps subject – verb.

head: Meaning
Chinese
Example
rows: 面包和牛奶 — never between two clauses
因为今天很冷，所以我们不去公园。
我们吃午饭，然后去公园。
我累的时候喜欢喝咖啡。
如果你饿了，我们就去吃饭。
虽然这个房子很小，但是很漂亮。
blocks.caption: Linking words

blocks.title: Pairs: both halves are marked
blocks.text: Chinese likes to mark both clauses: 因为…所以…, 虽然…但是…, 如果…就…. Either word may drop, but the pair is the clearest — and 虽然…但是… is correct Chinese, although English and German forbid ‘although … but’.

blocks.title: The word order never changes
blocks.text: After 因为, 如果 or 虽然 the clause keeps its normal order — subject, time, verb, object. German sends the verb to the end (weil ich müde bin); Chinese does not: 因为我很累.

blocks.caption: Condition first; 就 after the subject of the result

items.title: Before the subject: 但是 · 可是 · 所以 · 然后
Before or after the subject: 因为 · 如果 · 虽然
points: 如果你饿了… = 你如果饿了…
他虽然很累，可是很高兴。 (one subject for both clauses)

items.title: Right before the verb: 就
points: …，我们就吃饭。 — never *就我们吃饭

blocks.title: ‘When’ comes at the end
blocks.text: …的时候 closes its clause: 我饿的时候 ‘when I’m hungry’ — the opposite of English when and German wenn, which open it. The when-clause goes first in the sentence; in writing …时 is short for …的时候.

blocks.title: There is no ‘that’
blocks.text: 我知道他是老师 ‘I know (that) he is a teacher’, 我觉得这个很贵 ‘I think (that) this is expensive’ — the clause follows the verb directly. (知道 ‘know’, 觉得 ‘think’ and 说 ‘say’ come later.) Don’t translate ‘that’ with 那.

blocks.title: 和 does not join clauses
blocks.text: *我很累和我很饿 → 我很累，也很饿 (or just a comma). 和 joins nouns and pronouns: 我和你, 面包和牛奶.

blocks.title: 然后 and 以后
blocks.text: 然后 ‘then, after that’ joins two steps: 我们吃饭，然后去公园. 以后 ‘after’ closes a clause: 吃饭以后 ‘after eating’ (S15).

blocks.title: 的话 = if
blocks.text: …的话 at the end of a condition is ‘if’ on its own (你累的话，就回家吧) or together with 如果 (如果你累的话).

askYourself: Am I joining two clauses with ‘and’? → not 和: a comma, 也, or 然后 (‘and then’).
A contrast? → …，但是 / 可是 … at the start of the second clause.
A reason and a result? → 因为 …，所以 … (reason first).
Although? → 虽然 …，但是 / 可是 … — keep the second word.
A condition? → 如果 …（的话），subject + 就 + verb.
A time (when)? → clause + 的时候, at the start of the sentence.
‘That’ after know / think / say? → no word: the clause follows the verb.
Did I move the verb as in German? → put it back: the same order as in a main clause.
steps: Choose the pair (因为…所以, 虽然…但是, 如果…就) or the single word (但是, 然后, …的时候).
Keep subject – verb – object in each clause; 就 goes before the verb.

traps: *我很累和我很饿 → 我很累，也很饿.
*的时候我饿 → 我饿的时候 (的时候 after the clause).
*就我们去 → 我们就去 (就 after the subject).
*我们所以不去 → 所以我们不去 (所以 opens its clause).
*我知道那他是老师 → 我知道他是老师 (no ‘that’).
*因为很累我 → 因为我很累 (the order inside the clause stays subject – verb).
虽然…但是… is right in Chinese — don’t drop 但是 because English has no ‘but’ there.

quiz.why: 但是 opens the second clause; 和 never joins clauses.

options: 因为很冷，所以我们不去。
因为很冷，我们所以不去。
很冷因为，所以我们不去。
quiz.answer: 因为很冷，所以我们不去。
quiz.why: 因为 and 所以 open their clauses.

options: 如果你饿了，我们就吃饭。
如果你饿了，就我们吃饭。
你饿了如果，我们吃饭就。
quiz.answer: 如果你饿了，我们就吃饭。
quiz.why: 就 stands after the subject, right before the verb.

quiz.q: ‘Although the house is small, it is pretty.’
options: 虽然房子很小，但是很漂亮。
虽然房子小很，但是很漂亮。
quiz.answer: 虽然房子很小，但是很漂亮。
quiz.why: Both halves are marked: 虽然…但是….
Chinese has no ‘that’ before a clause.

seeAlso.note: German sends the verb to the end after weil, dass, wenn, obwohl (…, weil ich müde bin) and inverts after deshalb; Chinese keeps subject – verb order everywhere and marks both halves: 因为…所以….

Arabic لِأَنَّ ‘because’, أَنَّ ‘that’ and لٰكِنَّ ‘but’ need a noun in the accusative or a pronoun suffix right after them (لِأَنَّهُ مُتْعَبٌ ‘because he is tired’); Chinese 因为 takes a plain clause, and there is no ‘that’ at all.

Hebrew has a ‘that’, שֶׁ, attached to the clause (אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהוּא מוֹרֶה ‘I know that he is a teacher’), and כְּשֶׁ ‘when’, אִם ‘if’, כִּי ‘because’, לָכֵן ‘so’ — all at the START of the clause, where Chinese …的时候 comes at the end.
以前, 以后 and 的时候 after a clause (S15) are the same frame as ‘when’.
‘Or’: 还是 in questions, 或者 in statements (S09).
